 High interest rates have changed the income game. 
 Posted by 
 Sebastian Bowen 
 Author Bio 
 Sebastian Bowen has been a Motley Fool contributor since late 2018. Sebastian found his passion for writing and educating others about shares and all things finance after completing his studies in political, economic, and social science, and he enjoys bringing this passion to life at the Fool. His investment philosophy is simple – buying high-quality companies at sensible prices. When he’s not researching his next investment at all hours of the morning, Sebastian enjoys classic movies and unwinds with a good book, newspaper, or record.

 Favourite Investment Quote 
 " In the short run, the market is a voting machine, but in the long run, it is a weighing machine. "
– Benjamin Graham
 Published November 5, 3:45 pm AEDT 
 On Tuesday, we got the dramatic news that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has increased interest rates for the fifth time this year . At 4.85%, the cash rate is now at its highest level since late 2008 (let that one sink in).
 This is painful news for many people. Mortgage holders, of course, as well as any individuals or businesses with a floating loan or line of credit. But also the economy more broadly. Interest rates work to slow economic activity, which obviously doesn't bode well for many Australians. 
 With interest rates this high, the way we look at ASX shares as investments is quite different to how we may have when the cash rate was essentially zero a few years ago. 
 Back then, the appeal of ASX dividend shares was clear. They provided a real source of income, which, together with franking credits , was a clear advantage over cash-based investments. Not to mention real estate. Although real estate values skyrocketed during this zero-rate era, rental yields didn't really keep up. That left ASX shares as the primary way to secure real yield. 
 What a difference a few years makes. 
 With the cash rate now at 4.85%, the calculations look very different. The value of ASX shares has arguably held up quite well, given the steep climb that interest rates have been on in 2026. As it stands today, the S&P/ASX 200 Index (ASX: XJO) is pretty much at the level it was this time last year. 
 That means the  dividend yields  on many popular ASX income stocks remain relatively subdued. Sure, you can bag a fully-franked yield of over 4% from the likes of Westpac Banking Corp ( ASX: WBC ), National Australia Bank Ltd ( ASX: NAB ), and Telstra Group Ltd ( ASX: TLS ). But these companies are hardly growth engines. 
 Slightly more exciting dividend payers, like perhaps Commonwealth Bank of Australia ( ASX: CBA ), Wesfarmers Ltd ( ASX: WES ), or Washington H. Soul Pattinson and Co Ltd ( ASX: SOL ), currently offer yields well below 4%. 
 Image source: Getty Images
 High interest rates and ASX income stocks
 This might be acceptable for many ASX investors. After all, shares have consistently proven to be the most lucrative asset class to invest in long term. That's regardless of the rate of inflation , interest rates, or the health of the broader economy. However, for investors who prioritise yield and cash flow over overall returns, it might be a no-brainer to start branching out of stocks. 
 With the cash rate now at 4.85%, yields on cash-based assets are far higher than those offered by most ASX dividend shares. Consider the BetaShares Australian High Interest Cash ETF ( ASX: AAA ). This exchange-traded fund (ETF) is now offering a cash yield net of fees worth 4.92% per annum. That will probably rise even higher very soon. Since this ETF only holds cash-based assets issued by major ASX banks, there is virtually no risk of permanent capital loss if one invests in it. That's a compelling proposition for income-focused investors. 
 Another similarly structured ETF, the iShares Enhanced Cash ETF ( ASX: ISEC ), offers a similar option.
 The upside of higher interest rates is that one can achieve a real, risk-free yield from these kinds of ASX ETFs. You can also bypass the market entirely and open your own savings account or term deposit right now. You'll probably find you can snag an interest rate above 5.5% per annum if you look hard enough.
